newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama's leader says ex-U.S. bases to benefit all.
newsitem.headline: Panama's leader says ex-U.S. bases to benefit all.

text.p: Panamanian President Ernesto Perez Balladares pledged on Tuesday that former U.S. military bases being handed over to Panama would be transformed into economic projects to benefit all Panamanians, not just the rich.
He spoke at the handover ceremony of Fort Amador, a U.S. Second World War nerve centre which is to be turned into a chic tourist resort before the year 2000.
The Panamanian leader said there would be "no irresponsible or demagogic use of the lands. Future use will be determined by benefits to the economically needy."

Amador was put under Panamanian control in accordance with the Panama Canal treaties of 1977, under which the United States agreed to transfer control of the canal and surrounding military installations to Panama. Seven other U.S. bases will be handed over by Dec. 31, 1999 and 7,500 troops will pull out.

"There should be no doubts about our capacity to convert the military structures into new sources of employment and prosperity for the most collective and socially responsible uses possible," Perez Balladares said after receiving a symbolic key from Gen. Wesley Clark, commander-in-chief of the U.S. Southern Command military forces based in Panama.
Panama plans to transform Amador, located at the entrance of the Panama Canal on the Pacific side, into a $450-million hotel, cruise ship terminal and recreational complex.

A U.S.-South Korean consortium, United Enterprise Trust Group, recently signed an agreement with the government to develop a 12-story, 500-room luxury hotel on an island off Amador. The company will also build a monorail system, a shopping centre and 300 time-share apartments.
Construction on the site, a 15-minute drive from downtown Panama City, is scheduled to begin early next year.
